# Copper March 2012 - Copper prices continue to take their cue from a combination of macro-economic news and dollar movement rather than the fundamentals. Meanwhile, Chinese copper appetite appears to be in “go slow mode” compounded by rising inventories and imports. The key feature of the market is not so much price direction but rather the imbalance in the location of physical inventories which has led to tightness in the spreads. This has pushed premia higher in those locations where stocks are being consistently drawn down or tightly controlled such as Europe and the USA. - The stock overhang in China has capped LME prices throughout Q1 2012. As demand improves and stocks are drawn down through the year, prices will trade higher as 2012 records its third consecutive year of deficit of ~150kt. Growth in refined production of 3.4% will lag that of consumption to push metal stocks days of consumption lower to just 49 days by the year end. We still forecast an average price of $8700/t this year, with prices expected to trade at an average of $8900/t over the second half of 2012. - Key markets across the globe continue to make sequential improvements in demand, although these are on the prior month rather than necessarily on the year ago figure. Of particular note is the upturn in China, although this relatively modest upturn is far lower than apparent consumption calculations would suggest. A more bullish view on US demand has resulted in our global growth forecast rising to 3.7% this month, from 3.6% previously. - Supplies of concentrate remained constrained in March. Grasberg resumed production during the month following a three week outage, but the company reported that the shutdown had cost 80Mlb (36kt) of lost production. The appetite of Chinese smelters for incremental spot material appeared to wane in March, deterred by high stocks of refined metal, the unfavourable price arbitrage between the SHFE and LME cash price and low treatment and refining charges. In the long term market, the mating season moved towards a conclusion with Batu Hijau and OK Tedi are believed to have completed their negotiations at the Freeport benchmark levels of $63.5/t and 6.35c/lb. #### **Copper key forecasts** ||**2010**|**%**|**2011**|**%**|**2012**|**%**|**2013**|**%**| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |**Global (kt)**||||||||| |Total Mine Production|16177|1.4|16283|0.7|16982|4.3|18738|10.3| |Total Smelter Production|14759|4.2|15518|5.1|15934|2.7|17389|9.1| |Refined Production|19009|3.8|19698|3.6|20363|3.4|21993|8.0| |Consumption|19266|11.3|19791|2.7|20514|3.7|21428|4.5| |Concentrate Market Balance|227||-244||0||100|| |Metal Market Balance|-257||-93||-151||565|| |Metal Stocks-Days of Cons|57||54||49||57|| |**Prices**||||||||| |Cash LME Price ($/t)|7536||8810||8700||8150|| |(c/lb)|342||400||395||370|| |Contract TC/RCs (c/lb excl pp)|11.9||14.4||16.3||18.0|| |

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Macro rather than fundamental headlines direct LME prices…** Copper prices continue to take their cue from a combination of economic news and dollar movement while tightness in the physical market is pushing premia higher across Europe and the USA.  Chinese copper appetite appears to be in “go slow mode” compounded by rising inventories and imports. 

Copper prices have been on a rollercoaster ride over the past month.  The 3-month price traded to highs at the end of February of $8645/t only to lose ground and hit a low of $8295/t on 7<sup>th</sup> March following an official announcement by China's Prime Minister Wen Jiabao that the country was lowering its growth prospects to 7.5%, the lowest level in years. Although prices recovered to trade closer to the $8600/t mark by mid-month, a bout of disappointing PMIs out of China and Europe led to another dip in LME copper, pushing 3-month prices to lows of $8296/t at the end of last week.  China’s flash estimate of the HSBC manufacturing PMI was weaker than had been expected, slipping from 49.6 in February to 48.1 in March.  This was the sixth consecutive month of contraction and the worst for four months.  All the different subindices showed contraction, pointing to more weakness in the Chinese economy.  The Euro zone flash PMIs were also lower than had been expected.  The flash estimate of the Euro zone composite PMI slipped to 48.7 in March versus 49.3 in February.  Services activity was broadly stable (48.7 in March versus 48.8 in February) while the manufacturing PMI fell to a three month low of 47.7 versus 49.0 in February. 

LME copper climbed at the start of the week beginning 26<sup>th</sup> March amid signs of improvement in the U.S. economy and progress in containing Europe’s sovereign debt crisis.  The Federal Reserve Chairman’s comments about encouraging unemployment rates and the possibility of the central bank stimulating monetary policies boosting the 3-month LME price.  The slowdown in China’s manufacturing sector is still causing concern and worries are mounting that the appetite for copper from the world’s largest consumer could disappoint which continues to temper copper’s ascent short-term. 

**…as stock location imbalance leads to tighter spreads…** Indeed the key feature of the copper market at present is not so much price direction but rather the imbalance in the location of physical inventories which has led to tightness in the spreads.  Premia are higher in those locations where stocks are being consistently drawn down or tightly controlled. As prices swing in line with the macroeconomic news flows, an uptick in demand from the USA and a better than expected start to the year in Europe, have helped to support the LME price. 

Total exchange stocks currently stand at around 360kt, with the bulk of material, 50% held in US (L

ME and Comex) warehouses, 44% in Shanghai and Asian LME warehouses and just 6% held in Europe. SHFE stocks have built up steadily since the beginning of February, hitting a high of 227kt on 16th March, up at levels last seen in 2002. Meanwhile, stocks on both Comex and the LME have maintained a downward trend throughout March. At the time of writing stocks on the LME had fallen by just over 38kt to 258kt, with cancelled warrants of 84kt accounting for 33% of total stocks on the Exchange. The USA continues to see the largest draw downs, not surprising as this is where the bulk, 77%, of LME inventories are currently held. Of the total tonnage held in US LME warehouses, 38% is currently cancelled and therefore “unavailable” to the market. Comex stocks have fallen to 82kt, down by over 1.5kt in the past month. #### **Copper exchange stock movements** 150

Source: LM E, Comex, SHFE, Brook Hunt – A Wood M ackenzie Company **…which support higher premia in the USA and Europe…** As stocks continue to be drawn down amid signs of some improvement in demand in the USA, cathode premiums have ticked higher and have been quoted in a range of around 5-6 c/lb, on a delivered Mid-west basis. Some spot deals have been focussed in a narrower range of 5.25-5.75c/lb. This slight uptick in premiums is also reflecting higher trucking costs, inland transportation, combined with concerns over availability, given the difficulties getting metal out of exchange facilities. Moreover, the closure of one of Mexico’s copper refineries owned by Mexican billionaire Carlos Slim's Grupo Carso earlier this month, led to a rash of enquiries from domestic consumers looking for material. While the plant had not been producing at full capacity, its closure should see some additional spot demand for cathode and will likely contribute to the growing perception of tightness in North America, as could the impending planned maintenance shutdown of Rio Tinto's Kennecott Utah Copper's Garfield smelter in May. As noted above, interest in Europe has been better on the cathode front but has yet to feed through to higher semis production. Market participants are split, with some suggesting an

uptick in activity, while others suggest that it is simply consumers buying in the dips.  It is clear from our conversations that many European consumers booked much less material on contract for 2012 and are now scrambling to replenish some of their pipeline stocks.  As the producers do not have any spare copper units consumers have had to step into the spot market.  The persistent decline in inventories at European LME warehouses, down by 25% since the end of 2011, has supported the rising trend in premia over the past three months.  CIF Rotterdam premia are certainly up on the $60/t level we reported last month and have gradually progressed higher with cathode trade now up around the $90-100/t level and up from the $85-90/t range last week.  CIF Livorno has remained at $50-60/t, while premiums for CIS cathode have held at $0-30/t, depending on the quality of the cathode. 

With activity in the USA and Europe having picked up, this has been reflected in LME copper price spreads, with the cash to 3-month backwardation flaring out to highs of around $45-50/t early this week, compared to levels of $20-30/t last week.  Thus, it is not surprising that some material has finally been attracted into warehouses.  LME stocks rose for the first time since 21<sup>st</sup> February, up by 3.6kt on 26th March.  Rotterdam and Antwerp were the main beneficiaries, up by 2.3kt and 0.7kt respectively, likely aided by the rising physical premiums, while Singapore attracted around 1.3kt.  It remains to be seen if the backwardation persists and attracts sufficient quantities into Europe, where the metal is required. 

**February imports add to swollen Chinese inventories** Meanwhile spot interest from China is sporadic, switching from super bullish to totally quiet with premia for imported cathode subdued in the $20-50/t range, reflecting weak demand for imported cathode.  We understand that producers have locked in much larger volumes for China on a contract basis this year compared to 2011 levels and it is this contract volume that is appearing in the swollen Chinese import data.  Levels rose again in February, taking total imports over the first two months of 2012 up to 711kt, a staggering 76% over 2011 volumes.  As has been well reported, much of this refined material is ending up in bonded warehouse and held as collateral.  Our data suggests that in addition to the 224kt of cathode on the SHFE exchange, bonded warehouses are closer to the 600kt level.  Despite the lower prospects for GDP growth mentioned above and the build up of stocks in China, our outlook for refined copper demand in China this year is unchanged.  There are signs of improving semis production, while planned investment in the copper intensive distribution sector this year, rather than on transmission development of the power grid, will boost demand.  Also a forecast rebound in automotive production of c.7% after a sluggish start will shore up demand from this sector.

**A third consecutive year of deficit as refined production growth lags that of demand** We remain of the view that 2012 will record its third consecutive year of global deficit in the copper market of ~150kt. Growth in refined production of 3.4% will lag that of consumption to push metal stocks days of consumption lower to just 49 days compared to 54 days in 2011. The stock overhang in China has capped LME prices throughout Q1 2012. Although as demand improves and stocks are drawn down as we progress through the year, prices will trade higher, to average at $8700/t ($3.95/lb) for the full year. Even as refined consumption benefits from solid Chinese growth of 7% and an improving macro-economic environment elsewhere, growth in both mine and refined copper production will peak next year to push the market into a fully-fledged surplus of 565kt. As supply growth exceeds that of demand and metals stocks advance to average 57 days we expect to see prices come under pressure and now forecast 2013 prices to average $8150/t ($3.70/lb). #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai US c/lb 10

Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

Key markets across the globe continue to make sequential improvements in demand, although these are on the prior month rather than necessarily on the year ago figure.  Of particular note is the upturn in China, although this relatively modest upturn is far lower than apparent consumption calculations would suggest.  A more bullish view on US demand has resulted in our global growth forecast rising to 3.7% this month, from 3.6% previously. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Re-stocking provides first quarter boost** The sharp contraction in demand in the final part of 2011 was in part driven by de-stocking across supply chains as firms adopted a wait and see attitude amid economic uncertainty.  While the major stumbling blocks to resolving the euro debt crisis appear to have been mostly resolved it is probably a little premature to declare an outright end to the currency group’s troubles.  Significantly, businesses across the region, although most notably in Germany, seem to be placing orders again and this has led to an improvement in demand for copper in the first quarter of this year.  It is too early to state with any conviction whether this represents a recovery in consumption or that the upturn was simply re-stocking activity, although semis producers do feel a lot more upbeat about demand conditions. 

**Economic weakness to weigh on full year demand** The better near term demand conditions are not immediately obvious from our industrial production forecasts, which for much of Europe point to a contraction in output.  Indeed, Germany, France, Italy and Spain will all experience a decline in activity this year and even by 2013 we are still only forecasting growth of c.1% for these countries.  The negative industrial and economic backdrop will cast a dark pale over demand for copper and as such, we forecast contraction in regional demand this year, with only a modest improvement in 2013. 

**Russia to ease back after tax-induced surge** As we noted on a number of occasions during the past year, Russian apparent consumption of copper surged in 2011 as a result of the re-introduction of a tax on cathode at the start of that year.  The result was that rather than export refined copper, material was processed at home into wire rod, which was often then exported but this resulted in a massive increase in domestic consumption of refined copper even if the final product was then shipped abroad.  However, for this year we expect there to be a bit of a hangover in Russia as export markets for wire rod flag. 

**Electrical sector dented by solar weakness** Changes to feed-in tariffs in

Germany are leading to short term weakness in the solar segment of the electrical sector and this is tempering demand from what has been a red hot sector.  After rampant growth over the past few years boosted by generous feed-in tariffs, these have now been cut by around 30% and this is likely to hit sectoral growth in the short term.  The growth of this sector has attracted a lot of competition from solar cell producers and rationalisation is probably required before the next stage of growth can take place.  However, the longer term prospects remain healthy for green energy, particularly as nuclear power is becoming increasingly unpalatable. 

**Indicators pointing east for transport growth** The motor vehicle market will face a period of consolidation or even retrenchment this year after the sharp growth of 2010 and 2011.  In relatively uncertain economic times consumers are putting off purchases of vehicles and as such, production will also be hit, which explains our forecast of overall European vehicle production showing little to no growth in 2012.  The following years should see some improvement across the region but over the longer term growth will be focussed on eastern Europe, with Russia and Poland in particular enjoying strong growth. 

**Short term optimism but full year contraction** For the year as a whole we reiterate our negative view on demand, despite the steady start to the year.  Indeed, while the rise in regional premia could be viewed as a positive reflection of improving consumption, it is actually in part a result of semis producers taking a more cautious view on annual contracts this year given the uncertain outlook and using the spot market to top up requirements.  The better-than-expected order in take has resulted in some tightness in the spot market and driven premia to as much as $90/t.  However, despite the near term positive sentiment, we reiterate our expectation of a c.1% contraction in European demand this year. 

### **Americas** 

**Mildly positive macro-economic indicators support US copper…** If this first quarter of 2012 can be termed the epitome of mediocrity, the most encouraging one can say about it is that at least the vital signs sustaining metals in general have been mildly in the black.  Whether one looks at copper-related economic and sectoral data, such as IP figures or auto and housing data, or direct copper industry statistics, the conclusion for market watchers is that we have been in a mildly upward trend for many months.  For the metals business, this in itself is encouraging: we have seen no severe shocks and a consistent pattern of month on month of generally improving business conditions in North America at a time when LME copper quotes have been contained within a pretty narrow range since the middle of February.  In this financials-driven era of boom-bust headlines grabbing the news, such relative stability allows metals buyers the

chance to focus on the underlying demand fundamentals, rather than being preoccupied by accountants and metal stocks levels. 

**..bolstered by decreasing visible stocks at LME warehouses…** The main eye-catching development affecting the entire US copper sector over the past six weeks or so has been the visible draw-down in LME stocks, principally in warehouses in New Orleans and St Louis.  Since the start of the year, stocks in these LME locations have fallen from 233kt combined to 165kt, with a further 70kt combined now on cancelled warrant; there has been little change in Comex stocks either.  While the reasons behind such a stock drop range from the possibility that one market player has been caught short to en masse Chinese exports given the concomitant rise in Shanghai stocks, the end result of importance to North American consumers has been increasing concern over metal availability.  Premia for copper delivered mid-west have trended to the upper end of the 5.25-5.75c/lb range, while reportedly north east premia have approached 6c/lb. Transport logistics have contributed to this upward momentum, however, so it is not always a straightforward translation that higher premia stem from higher metal demand. 

**..and concern over supply from the dwindling number of regional refineries** But other evidence suggests that metal is getting tighter: one South American producer told us, for example, that he has exported cathode to the USA for the first time in a couple of years, indicating that the customer base may be getting somewhat anxious about supply on the one hand, and that sufficiently strong premia exist to warrant the trade.  To that, we would also remind readers that we have seen refinery closures in the region over the past few years, and this may well contribute to a regional pinch during, arguably, the first time of improving demand since the 2008 crash _and_ post-refinery closures.  In 2010, the Canadian Kidd Creek and the US White Pine both closed, taking c.170kt/a capacity offline; this year, we were expecting Condumex’s Cobre de Mexico to close as well, and indications are that it has already been shuttered, removing another 70kt/a capacity from the region.  As we move further into the year, though, this tightness should be somewhat eased by higher cathode output from refineries across Canada and the USA, despite the well-advertised drop in output from Garfield due to the temporary ore grade decline).  We are expecting 7% stronger refined output this year in North America than last, but some of the more prominent sources should contribute higher tonnages only from H2. 

**Construction market stable, autos finds fifth gear** From the demand side, the US housing market continues to show the same degree of stability that we have come to appreciate and interpret as “good news”, given the dreadful slump seen in 2009: home prices were unchanged month-on-month in January, which was the first time sin

ce last July that they have not declined. And despite the 0.9% drop in existing home sales in February, the mild winter across the USA assisted in providing the best sales for the first two months of this year than in the past five years. In the automotive sector, while sales of light trucks in the USA increased by 7.6% in February over the prior month (and by 5.8% over a year ago), car sales increased by almost 24% last month and by 22% over February 2011, lending credence to the anticipated high replacement rates that we have discussed previously. Although official production data for the copper rod sector has yet to come available for January, rod producers continue to have confidence in stronger markets this year than last. If the sector does realize the near 5% improvement in business this year that some rod producers tell us that they expect, this would return national output to just shy of mid2008 levels (i.e. pre-crash). Meanwhile, data for January from the Copper and Brass Service Association are equally encouraging. Its members revealed shipments that were 26.9% higher than December (not surprising, given the destocking effect customary at the end of the year), and 13.7% up on those seen in January 2011. #### **US Copper and Brass Service center shipments – (kt)** 12000 Tonnes

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - March 2012 Page 7 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **China** **Slow start speeds up in March** It is fair to say that semis production and therefore refined demand have improved in March, although the upturn has been more muted than would have been hoped for. Output in the first two months of the year was hit by high stocks of finished goods and sluggish demand in end use markets, which ultimately hit semis production. However, the current tepid demand conditions have not altered our conviction of a second half upswing and 8% growth for the full year. Semis production in March is better than in the first 2 months, but the overall situation is still relatively sluggish. Initial indications are the wire rod production in March is up by 20% on levels in February, but this would mean that mills are still only operating at around 80% capacity. Falling aircon and auto production hit demand for magnet wire, although power cable demand ought to improve by April now that funds for power grid projects are being allocated. Sheet and strip demand improved significantly in March compared with the levels of January and February, but was still lower than a year ago. Falling auto production impacted demand for high-end connector strip. Most connector makers are still very cautiously managing their inventories because of tight working cap

ital, unexpectedly low order books and falling profit margins. **Imports surge overstates consumption** Set against broad market expectations of a slowdown, imports of refined copper yet again surprised on the upside in February, rising by 138% year on year to 375.8kt. Taking the first two months of the year together, imports are up a relatively sedentary 76% to 711.3kt. When combined with a strong uplift in production, according to CNIA data, apparent consumption rose by an impressive 35% in the January to February period to 1460kt. This figure includes SHFE stock movements but does not account for the increase in stocks elsewhere, however. We estimate that unreported stocks rose by c.400kt by the end of February and thus, real consumption is therefore significantly lower, although still in positive territory when compared with a year ago. **Distribution to power up electrical sector demand** The State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC) announced that its planned investment growth in the power grid would be 2.6% in 2012. However, the focus will be transferred from the transmission sector to the distribution sector, which is more copper intensive. Indeed, we forecast a strong contribution from the power sector to our Chinese growth forecast this year. **Autos to pick up speed** The automotive market has endured a sluggish start to 2012 although we still forecast an improvement on the lacklustre pace of growth in 2011. Last year was always expected to be a year of consolidation for the Chinese automotive market following the stellar growth of the previous two years and indeed, total vehicle production rose by a modest 1% to 18.4 million units. For 2012, however, we forecast a rebound in production of c.7%, with similar growth expected in 2013 and 2014. **Overhang of end use products hits consumer and HVAC** Consumer and HVAC markets face the same problems this year that the automotive market endured in 2011, with the sectors set to face a hangover from sharp growth stemming from purchase incentive schemes. This resulted in production of white goods rising by 12% last year, while air conditioner output surged by an even more impressive 26%, although we expect low single-digit growth in output this year given an overhang of end use products and sluggish domestic and export demand. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

The 1.2% year-on-year rise to 59.4kt was dwarfed by the 6.1% increase on the prior month as most key end use sectors chipped in to the rise. Meanwhile, the Japanese Copper and Brass Association have stated their expectation of a 2.4% rise in brass mill production in the upcoming Japanese financial year and while this does not tally exactly with our calendar year forecast, the growth rates are in line with our c.2% forecast for refined copper consumption growth. **Electrical sector lacks spark in short term** The key electrical and electronics sector has been dealt a heavy blow by the nuclear disaster which has resulted in energy producers scaling back investment as they deal with the closure of nuclear power stations. This is hitting demand for copper products from the sector in the short term, although this ought to at least provide a boost to demand, possibly from 2014 onwards as deferred investment takes place. At the same time, demand for electronic products is being hit by weakness in key export markets, although this too should stage a recovery in line with global economic activity over the next few years. In particular, demand for copper foil is flagging presently across key electronics markets, with demand from lithium Ion batteries for cars the one bright spot in the short term. **Construction to enjoy near term upturn** The long term decline of the Japanese construction market may be interrupted by a blip upwards over the next year or so as reconstruction efforts temporarily provide a boos

t to demand but even this will only be relatively modest. In fact, after enjoying something of an improvement through the middle of last year, housing starts are now on the wane again, having posted five consecutive year-on-year declines through to January of this year. **Auto sector continues to accelerate** The automotive market is unarguably the bright spot in the Japanese market as production of automobiles recovers from the disruptions of the previous year. Those disruptions are well documented but the key point is that car production fell by 13.9% last year, although is set to recover strongly in 2012, expanding at a similar rate to leave 2012 output just a little shy of 2010 production. Indeed, Japanese car sales have got off to a good start this year, up by 35% in the January to February period. The copper smelter, rated to handle 300k dmt/a of concentrate, forms part of a metallurgical complex that also includes lead and zinc smelters, copper and lead refineries, a precious metals refinery, and antimony, bismuth, indium and arsenic trioxide plants.  The copper smelter, therefore, has considerable flexibility to treat concentrates from local mines with a high precious metal content and also significant levels of impurities such as lead, zinc, arsenic and antimony. Since the complex closed in 2009 due to cash f

low problems, the concentrates previously treated there have been sold to traders for blending.  Re-opening the smelter should lead to higher quality concentrates, no longer needed for blending, being available for export from Peru.

## Blister/anode and scrap markets 

**China scrap imports rise marginally, but demand is muted** According to customs statistics, copper scrap imports into China for the first two months of the year were 632kt, a 3.5% increase over the same period in 2011.  Imports were inhibited by the negative price arbitrage between the SHFE and LME (averaging -$315/t in February) and falling local discounts for No.2 scrap of around 3000 to 3500RMB/t (22 to 25c/lb) in March compared with 4000 to 4500RMB/t (29 to 32c/lb) in late January.  Anecdotally, No.2 scrap is reported to be freely available on European markets as a result of reduced demand from China. Both parcels are understood to be destined for China.

## Production news 

**Mine output in Peru drops in January** Following the announcement at the start of this month that Chilean copper production fell by 7.6% in January this year _vs._ 2011, Peru Ministry of Mines released details of a similar drop in output. Mine production fell by 5% in January to 97.8kt compared to the same month last year (102.7kt), with improvements at Antamina and Toquepala insufficient to offset losses at Cerro Verde and Tintaya.  With its US$1.288Bn expansion programme now kicking in, Antamina’s copper in concentrate output rose by almost 19% to 28.1kt.  We expect full year output to build to 450kt this year, from 334kt in 2011 (+35%).  Southern Peru Copper Corp’s Toquepala managed a 70% improvement at its mill operations (7.1kt this January, _vs._ 4.2kt a year ago), although its SxEw plant saw output collapse by 90% to just 56t from 573t.  Toquepala is also going through an expansion programme which, the company says, should add 100kt/a copper in concentrate capacity from early 2014.  SPCC’s Cuajone division increased output by almost 5% at its mill to 12kt, which is just shy of our expected 147kt contained in concentrate target for the year. Freeport’s Cerro Verde, which was expected to see output fall this year by 5% from 2011’s 303kt from mill and SxEw facilities, has already witnessed a 37% decline in mill output (14.7kt _vs._ 23.5kt) and a 3% drop in cathode output (6.2 _vs._ 6.4kt) in January.  Xstrata’s Tintaya also fell by 15.4% at the mill comparing the months, from 4.7kt to 4kt, while cathode production dropped even more precipitously from 2kt to just 700t. 

**Stop-start Grasberg resumes production mid-month** Freeport confirmed on March 15<sup>th</sup> that it had been able to restart operations at its Indonesian Grasberg mine and mill after the labour stoppage that began February 23<sup>rd</sup> and that intermittent interruptions on operations had now been resolved.  This latest setback, after two significant outages last year, has cost an est

imated 80Mlbs of copper and 125kozs of gold.  Freeport believes full output operating rates will be achieved once again during the second quarter.

The drilling programme has identified a P&P mineral reserve of 774Mt at 0.5% Cu, using a 0.2% Cu cut-off. **Indonesia presses ahead for mineral upgrade plans** The Indonesian government is continuing to press ahead with its stated aim of blocking exports of semi-processed mineral products by January 2014.  All minerals and coal will have to undergo various beneficiation stages to remain within the law and retain an appropriate license from the government to operate, and in the case of copper the minimum grade of a copper product that will be able to leave the country is 99%. This effectively means only anode/cathode copper can be exported, which places some doubt over the exports of existing concentrate.  The law remains

unclear, though, on the status of existing operators.  For now, the government’s Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry has received dozens of requests from mine operators looking to receive permission to upgrade their plants, or from new ventures looking to take advantage of what might become newly available feed materials.  This has brought to light at least two copper smelting/refining plants, and possibly now a third. PT Indosmelting has been looking to set up a 100kt/a processing facility at Maros, South Sulawesi for a number of years, while PT Nusantara Smelting wants to do the same with a 200kt/a plant at Bontang, East Kalimantan.  Now PT Global Perkasa Investindo is considering building a 400kt/a smelting-refining complex at Timika, on Papua.  PT Batutua Tembaga Raya’s plans for the 25kt/a Wetar will be unaffected by the new legislation because it intends to leach its ores through to cathode, starting later this year.  Even so, and ignoring the fact that prevailing TC/RCs are far too low to justify greenfield smelter/refinery developments in that country, this proposed additional 700kt/a smelting-refining capacity is expected to have a difficult time obtaining suitable feed material unless the government is legally able to overturn the ability of the nation’s two principal copper concentrate exporters (Freeport’s Grasberg and Newmont’s Batu Hijau) to send some of their product overseas, as we do not see any significant new mine developments within Indonesia on the horizon which would provide concentrate.
